title: A Holistic approach to understand the immunometabolic Pathomechanisms of Endometriosis
summary:
Endometriosis is a chronic inflammatory disease affecting women that often remains undiagnosed for a long time and for which there is currently no cure. Affected women experience a substantial burden of disease caused by chronic and cyclic severe pain, infertility, abdominal bloating and swelling, gastrointestinal problems, food intolerances, chronic fatigue, and psychological distress—both as a result of the disease itself and of inadequate treatment options.
Previous research into the causes of endometriosis has insufficiently addressed this broad spectrum of symptoms and their underlying causes. The HoPE research consortium therefore pursues a holistic, systems biology-based approach to better understand the disease, develop more effective treatment strategies, and reduce the burden experienced by affected women in the long term.
The study focuses on the interactions between diet, the immune system, energy metabolism, the gut microbiome, psychological factors, and psychological stressors (including depression, anxiety, stress, trauma, and fatigue), and their influence on inflammatory and hormonal processes in endometriosis. Particular attention is paid to food intolerances, nutritional status, the gut bacterial profile, and the energy metabolism of immune cells—factors that have often been neglected in clinical practice to date. To this end, women with endometriosis and healthy control participants will undergo a comprehensive one-time assessment of these factors and symptoms.
The aim of the HoPE consortium is to investigate the biomolecular pathomechanisms of endometriosis. The project examines the interplay between stress and nutritional factors, the immune system, energy metabolism of immune cells, food intolerances, the gut microbiome, and the estrobolome in order to better understand the inflammatory and hormonal mechanisms underlying endometriosis. Based on the findings and incorporating feedback from patients, innovative dietary concepts will be developed in the future and their suitability as an adjunctive treatment for endometriosis will be evaluated. A deeper understanding of the disease and its causes is intended to contribute to the development of new treatment options in the long term.
A key objective is the future development of personalized dietary concepts aimed at improving endometriosis symptoms. By analyzing dietary records, nutritional status parameters, and food intolerances, patients with similar patterns will be grouped into clusters. Targeted dietary programs will subsequently be developed for these groups and evaluated for the first time in a follow-up study to assess their effectiveness.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Patients with a sonographically and/or surgically (histologically) confirmed diagnosis of endometriosis (N80.x), i.e., including endometriosis of the uterus – adenomyosis (N80.0), the ovary (N80.1), the fallopian tube (N80.2), the pelvic peritoneum (N80.3), the rectovaginal septum and vagina (N80.4), the intestine (N80.5), in a skin scar (N80.6), other endometriosis (N80.8), and endometriosis, unspecified (N80.9).

premenopausal
Exclusion criteria:
Pregnancy
Presence of an active or previous cancer diagnosis
Use of immunosuppressive medications or therapies
Diagnosis of AIDS (Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome)
Current or previous diagnosis of hepatitis (including hepatitis B, hepatitis C, or other forms)
Treatment with Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) as part of their care within 4 weeks prior to study enrollment
